button-name.whatItMeans: A submit button only shows an arrow icon, and that icon is hidden from assistive tech, so the button has no readable label at all.
button-name.whoItAffects: Someone using a screen reader lands on the button and hears just 'button' with no clue what it does, so they can't confidently submit the form.
button-name.howToFix: Add visible or screen-reader-only text inside the button, like 'Submit', or add an aria-label="Submit" attribute to the button element.

image-alt.whatItMeans: An image on the page has no alternative text describing what it is.
image-alt.whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear nothing useful (often just the filename or 'image') and have no idea what the picture shows or why it's there.
image-alt.howToFix: Add an alt attribute to the img tag describing its content, or if it's purely decorative, use alt="" so screen readers skip it.

label.whatItMeans: An email input field has no associated label telling users what to type into it.
label.whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear only 'edit text' with no indication it's for an email address, making the form confusing or unusable.
label.howToFix: Add a <label> element linked to the input via a matching 'for' and 'id' attribute, such as <label for="email">Email</label>.

select-name.whatItMeans: A dropdown menu for choosing a plan (Free/Pro) has no name or label announced to assistive technology.
select-name.whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear just 'combo box' with no idea it's for selecting a subscription plan, so they may pick the wrong option or skip it.
select-name.howToFix: Add a <label> element for the select, or an aria-label attribute like aria-label="Choose plan", so its purpose is announced.

color-contrast.whatItMeans: Some text — like 'Read our terms before continuing,' the promotional banner, and 'All sales final' — is too light or too close in color to its background, making it hard to read.
color-contrast.whoItAffects: People with low vision, color blindness, or anyone viewing the screen in bright light will struggle to read this text, potentially missing important terms or offers.
color-contrast.howToFix: Darken the text color or change the background so the contrast ratio meets at least 4.5:1 for normal text, per WCAG guidelines.

document-title.whatItMeans: The web page has no title set in the browser tab or window.
document-title.whoItAffects: Screen reader users and people with many browser tabs open can't identify the page by name, and it hurts search engine listings too.
document-title.howToFix: Add a descriptive <title> element inside the page's <head>, such as <title>Pricing – YourCompany</title>.

html-has-lang.whatItMeans: The page's HTML code doesn't declare what language the content is written in.
html-has-lang.whoItAffects: Screen readers may guess the wrong language and pronounce the text with an incorrect accent or mispronunciation, making it hard to understand.
html-has-lang.howToFix: Add a lang attribute to the opening <html> tag, for example <html lang="en"> for English.

link-name.whatItMeans: A link pointing to the pricing page has no visible text or label, so it appears empty.
link-name.whoItAffects: Screen reader users hear just 'link' with no destination information, leaving them unsure where it goes or whether to click it.
link-name.howToFix: Add descriptive text inside the link, such as 'View pricing,' or provide an aria-label="View pricing" if the link uses only an icon.
